opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the really interesting open questions. Right now, a lot of the reasoning these models do is in text, and that makes sense, because language is where the pre-training is richest and it's a very compact, compositional representation. But if you think about how a person actually plans a physical task, a lot of it isn't verbal. When you reach for a cup on a cluttered table, you're not narrating "move the hand left three centimeters." You have some kind of spatial, predictive picture of what's going to happen.

So I think there's real potential in letting robots, and models in general, represent intermediate steps in whatever modality fits the problem. Sometimes that's language: high-level decomposition like "first open the drawer, then pick up the sponge." Sometimes it's something closer to images or video: imagining what the scene should look like after a step, and using that as a subgoal. And sometimes it's something more abstract, a latent representation that isn't directly human-interpretable but captures the dynamics well enough to support planning.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming we have to hand-design which modality goes where. The lesson of the last decade is that when you let the model learn its own representations, given enough data and the right objective, it tends to find something better than what you'd engineer. Language is a wonderful scaffold because it ties into all that internet knowledge, but I'd expect the most capable systems to fluidly mix verbal reasoning with more grounded, predictive, visual or physical reasoning, and to learn when each is useful.

There's also a practical angle. Text-based chain of thought gives you interpretability, which is valuable, especially for robots operating around people. If more of the reasoning moves into latent or visual spaces, we'll need new tools to understand what the system is actually planning. That's a tradeoff worth taking seriously, not just from a performance standpoint but from a safety and trust standpoint.

r001.rationale: The response says models should learn to represent intermediate steps in whichever modality fits the problem, giving language, images or video, and latent representations as examples for planning and reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually one of the more interesting and underexplored questions. When we think about language models, there's this very natural way they represent plans and reasoning: they just write it out in text. Chain of thought is a plan written in natural language. And that works remarkably well because language is a very compressed, very general representation that humans designed specifically for communicating abstract ideas.

But if you think about what a robot needs to do, a lot of the relevant structure in the world isn't really linguistic. If I'm trying to figure out how to grasp a mug that's wedged behind a coffee maker, the "reasoning" I'm doing is largely spatial. I'm imagining where my hand goes, what the clearances are, what happens if I rotate the mug a little. Describing that in words is possible, but it's awkward and lossy. So one thing I'm quite excited about is whether we can have models reason in modalities that are closer to the structure of the problem. You could imagine a model that generates a little video of what it expects to happen, or a sequence of intermediate images or keypoints, and uses that as its scratchpad rather than text.

There's a nice analogy to how people work. We clearly do some reasoning verbally, but we also do a lot of visual and motor imagination. Athletes rehearse movements mentally. When you plan how to pack a suitcase, you're not writing sentences in your head, you're picturing things fitting together. So I think the right answer is probably that different parts of a plan want different representations, and a really capable system should be able to move between them. Language is great for the high-level, discrete, "what am I even trying to do" part. Something more continuous and perceptual is probably better for the "how exactly does this play out physically" part.

The challenge, honestly, is that we don't have the equivalent of the internet for those other modalities in the same way. Text on the internet is full of people explaining their reasoning, so a language model gets a lot of supervision for how to think in words. Videos on the internet show outcomes, but they don't show the intermediate reasoning that led to them. So part of the research problem is figuring out how to get a model to learn to use, say, a visual imagination as a reasoning tool when nobody has written down what that should look like. I suspect a lot of that will have to come from the model's own experience, from actually acting in the world and discovering which imagined futures were useful for making good decisions. That's where the reinforcement learning side of this becomes important, because it gives you a way to reward reasoning that leads to success rather than reasoning that looks like something a human wrote.

r001.rationale: The response proposes that models reason in modalities suited to the problem’s structure, such as visual or motor representations for physical planning, alongside language for high-level goals.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there, particularly when the reasoning concerns the physical world. If you’re trying to figure out how to pick up an object, you could describe the entire process in language, but that’s a somewhat awkward representation. A lot of what matters is geometry: where your hand is, where the object is, what’s going to collide with what. A representation that preserves that spatial structure could be much more useful.

For example, you could imagine a system that reasons by predicting images of possible future states. What would the scene look like if I moved this object out of the way? Would that let me reach the thing behind it? Those predictions could serve as intermediate steps in a plan. They wouldn’t necessarily have to be images that a person could look at. They could be internal representations that retain the information needed to choose an action.

Language has some very useful properties, though. It lets you abstract away details. If I say, ‘Go to the kitchen and get a glass of water,’ I don’t have to specify every movement along the way. So I suspect you want a combination: language for some of the more abstract reasoning, spatial or visual representations for other parts, and perhaps actions themselves as part of the representation.

The interesting question is whether we should prescribe those representations or let them emerge through learning. My inclination is to give the system enough flexibility to discover what works. But then you need a training objective that rewards reasoning that actually helps you accomplish the task. Producing a plausible-looking future is useful only to the extent that it helps you make a better decision.

r001.rationale: The response says representations could emerge through learning and that the system should have flexibility to discover what works, with training rewarding reasoning that helps accomplish the task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there, especially when you’re talking about systems that need to interact with the physical world. Language is a very useful representation for some kinds of reasoning, but it’s not obvious that it’s the right representation for everything.

If you’re trying to figure out how to pick up a cup, you could describe a plan in words: move your hand over here, close your fingers, lift it up. But that description leaves out almost everything that actually matters for executing the motion. A visual representation, or some learned representation of how the scene will change, could capture a lot of that much more naturally.

One possibility is that predicting a future observation is itself a kind of planning. If I can imagine what the scene should look like after I’ve completed part of a task, that gives me a subgoal. Then a lower-level controller can figure out how to get there. You could have language for the overall objective, images for intermediate goals, and actions for the details of execution.

The interesting question is whether we should prescribe those representations or let the model learn them. Human-readable representations are useful because we can inspect them and provide supervision. But there’s no particular reason to expect that the most effective internal representation for a robot will always be something that a person can read. I’d expect useful systems to move between representations, depending on what part of the problem they’re solving.

r001.rationale: The response presents visual or learned representations of scene changes as useful for planning and execution, and says systems should move between representations according to the task.
